description: A 17-chapter course based on the Tutorialspoint Compiler Design tutorial: compiler architecture and phases, lexical analysis, regular expressions, finite automata, syntax analysis, top-down and bottom-up parsing, error recovery, semantic analysis, runtime environments, symbol tables, intermediate code, code generation and optimization. summary: A compiler translates code written in one language into another language without changing the meaning. It is also expected to make the target code efficient in time and space.
Compiler design covers translation, error detection and recovery. The front end is lexical, syntax and semantic analysis; the back end is code generation and optimization.

A whole language processing system has more parts: a preprocessor, the compiler, an assembler, a linker and a loader. Related tools are the interpreter, the cross-compiler and the source-to-source compiler.

items: A compiler translates the code written in one language into some other language without changing the meaning of the program. It is also expected that a compiler should make the target code efficient and optimized in terms of time and space.

Compiler design principles give an in-depth view of the translation and optimization process. They cover basic translation mechanisms and error detection and recovery. The front end consists of lexical, syntax and semantic analysis. The back end consists of code generation and optimization.

To follow the course you need a basic understanding of at least one programming language. Exposure to assembly programming helps. The labs are in Python, and they build small working versions of the real components.

Source code does not become a running program in one step. A language processing system chains several tools. The first is the preprocessor. It runs before the compiler proper, and handles directives such as macro expansion and file inclusion.

The compiler then translates the result into assembly language or another target. The assembler turns assembly into machine code in an object file. The linker merges object files, and the loader puts the executable in memory.

The interpreter, like a compiler, translates high-level language into lower-level form. The difference is in how it reads input. A compiler reads the whole source at once, creates tokens, checks semantics, generates intermediate code and may involve many passes.
An interpreter reads a statement, converts it to intermediate code, executes it, then takes the next statement.
The error behaviour differs as well. If an error occurs, an interpreter stops execution and reports it, whereas a compiler reads the whole program even if it meets several errors.
The assembler translates assembly language into machine code. Its output is an object file, which contains machine instructions and the data needed to place them in memory.
The linker is a program that links and merges various object files to make an executable file. These files may have been produced by separate assemblers.

Its major task is to search for and locate the referenced modules and routines, and to decide where the code will be loaded, so the instructions can have absolute references. A reference that no object file defines is an unresolved symbol and the link fails.

The loader is part of the operating system. It is responsible for loading executable files into memory and executing them. It calculates the size of the program, creates memory space for it, and initializes registers to start execution.

A cross-compiler runs on a platform A and generates executable code for a platform B. Phone apps are usually built this way, on a desktop. A source-to-source compiler takes source code in one language and produces source code in another.
In the practice section you write a tiny linker. It follows references from a main module, collects the modules it needs, and reports an unresolved symbol if one is missing.

items: A compiler can broadly be divided into two parts, based on the way they compile: the analysis phase and the synthesis phase.

The analysis phase is known as the front end. It reads the source program, divides it into core parts, and then checks for lexical, grammar and syntax errors. It generates an intermediate representation of the source program and a symbol table, which are fed to the synthesis phase as input.
The synthesis phase is known as the back end. It generates the target program with the help of the intermediate representation and the symbol table.

This split is the reason one compiler family can support many languages and many machines. A new language needs a new front end. A new machine needs a new back end. The intermediate representation is the meeting point, and the symbol table travels with it.

A compiler can have many phases and passes. A pass refers to the traversal of a compiler through the entire program. A phase is a distinguishable stage which takes input from the previous stage, processes it and yields output that can be used as input for the next stage.
A pass can have more than one phase.

For example, a one-pass compiler might do lexing, parsing and code generation together while reading the file once. A multi-pass compiler builds a tree in the first pass and optimizes it in later passes.

summary: Compilation is a sequence of phases. Each takes input from the previous phase, has its own representation of the program and feeds the next. The phases are lexical analysis, syntax analysis, semantic analysis, intermediate code generation, code optimization and code generation.

The lexical analyzer turns characters into tokens. The parser turns tokens into a parse tree. The semantic analyzer checks the rules of the language. The code generators then produce, improve and finally map code to the target machine.
The symbol table is a data structure maintained through all phases. It stores identifier names with their types and supports scope management.

items: The compilation process is a sequence of phases. Each phase takes input from its previous stage, has its own representation of the source program, and feeds its output to the next phase of the compiler.

Lexical analysis is the first phase. The scanner works as a text scanner: it reads the source code as a stream of characters and converts it into meaningful lexemes. The analyzer represents these lexemes as tokens of the form token-name and attribute-value.
Syntax analysis, or parsing, comes next. It takes the tokens produced by lexical analysis and generates a parse tree, also called a syntax tree.
The token arrangements are checked against the grammar of the language: the parser checks whether the expression made by the tokens is syntactically correct.

Semantic analysis checks whether the parse tree follows the rules of the language. For example, assignment between compatible data types, and adding a string to an integer. It also keeps track of identifiers, their types and expressions, and whether identifiers are declared before use.
It produces an annotated syntax tree.

After semantic analysis the compiler generates intermediate code for an abstract machine. It sits between the high-level language and the machine language. It should be generated so that it is easy to translate into the target machine code.
Code optimization removes unnecessary code lines and arranges the sequence of statements to speed up execution without wasting resources such as CPU and memory.

In code generation, the generator takes the optimized intermediate code and maps it to the target machine language. It produces a sequence of, generally, relocatable machine code that performs the same task as the intermediate code.

The symbol table is a data structure maintained throughout all the phases. All the identifiers' names and their types are stored in it. It makes it easy for the compiler to search for an identifier record and retrieve it quickly, and it is also used for scope management.

Here is one statement through the first phases. The text x = a + 2 becomes the tokens id, equals, id, plus and number. The parser groups them into an assignment with a sum. The semantic analyzer checks that x and a are declared and compatible. The later chapters implement each phase in turn.

summary: Lexical analysis is the first phase. It takes the preprocessed source, removes whitespace and comments, and breaks it into tokens. An invalid token is a lexical error. It works closely with the syntax analyzer, which asks for tokens when it needs them.

A lexeme is the matched text. A pattern, written as a regular expression, says which lexemes make a valid token. Keywords, constants, identifiers, strings, numbers, operators and punctuation are all tokens.
An alphabet is a finite set of symbols, a string a finite sequence of them, and a language a set of strings. When scanning is ambiguous the longest match wins, and reserved words beat identifiers.

glossary.def: The actual characters matched in the source, such as value.
A rule describing what lexemes belong to a token, given by a regular expression.
A category of lexeme such as identifier or keyword, with an optional attribute.
Any finite set of symbols.
A finite sequence of symbols from an alphabet. The empty string is written epsilon.
A set of strings over an alphabet.
The scanner takes the longest lexeme that matches any token pattern.
When two patterns match the same lexeme, the earlier or reserved one wins, so keywords beat identifiers.

keyPoints: The lexer removes whitespace and comments and reports invalid tokens.
int value = 100; has the tokens int, value, =, 100 and ;.
Patterns are regular expressions; lexemes are the matched text.

items: Lexical analysis is the first phase of a compiler. It takes the modified source code from the language preprocessors, written as sentences. The lexical analyzer breaks these into a series of tokens, removing any whitespace or comments.

If the lexical analyzer finds a token invalid, it generates an error. It works closely with the syntax analyzer. It reads character streams from the source code, checks for legal tokens, and passes the data to the syntax analyzer when it demands.

A lexeme is a sequence of characters, alphanumeric, in a token. There are predefined rules for every lexeme to be identified as a valid token. These rules are defined by grammar rules, by means of a pattern.
A pattern explains what can be a token, and patterns are defined by means of regular expressions.
In programming languages, keywords, constants, identifiers, strings, numbers, operators and punctuation symbols can be considered tokens.
For example in C, the declaration int value = 100; contains the tokens int, a keyword; value, an identifier; the equals sign, an operator; 100, a constant; and the semicolon, a symbol.

Now the language-theory terms. An alphabet is any finite set of symbols. Binary has 0 and 1. Hexadecimal has the digits and the letters A to F. A string is any finite sequence of symbols. Its length is the number of symbols, so the length of tutorialspoint is 14.
A string of zero length is the empty string, written with the Greek letter epsilon.

A typical high-level language has these symbol groups. Arithmetic symbols: plus, minus, modulo, multiplication, division. Punctuation: comma, semicolon, dot, arrow. Assignment is the equals sign, and special assignments are plus-equals and its relatives.
Comparison operators are double equals, not equals, less than and so on. There are logical operators, shift operators, the preprocessor hash and the location specifier ampersand.

A language is a finite set of strings over some finite alphabet. Computer languages are treated as sets, so set operations such as union and concatenation can be applied. Finite languages can be described by regular expressions.
Now the longest match rule. The lexical analyzer scans the code letter by letter, and when it meets a whitespace, an operator symbol or a special symbol, it decides that a word is complete.

Take int intvalue; While reading the characters of the second word, up to int, the analyzer cannot know whether it has the keyword int or the start of the identifier intvalue. The longest match rule says: choose the longest lexeme that matches any token. Here that is intvalue, an identifier.

The analyzer also follows rule priority. A reserved word of the language has priority over user input. If the lexeme int is exactly a keyword, it becomes a keyword token, so a programmer cannot use it as a variable name. The tutorial words this as the analyzer generating an error.
In practice, the scanner emits the keyword token, and the parser or semantic analysis rejects the misuse as an identifier.
In the practice section you write a real tokenizer. It applies the longest match rule, gives keywords priority, skips whitespace, and handles two-character operators like double equals.

practice.title: A tokenizer
practice.intro: Write tokenize(src). Split the source text into tokens, skipping whitespace. Return a list of [kind, lexeme]. Kinds: "KEYWORD" for int, float, if, else, while, return; "ID" for a letter or underscore followed by letters, digits or underscores (take the longest match, then check for a keyword); "NUM" for digits; "OP" for == != <= >= and the single characters + - * / = < > !; "PUNCT" for ; , ( ) { }. A character that fits nothing gives ["ERROR", char].
practice.hint: Loop with an index i. Look at the character: letter, digit, two-character operator, one-character operator or punctuation. For words take the longest run of letters and digits, then test the keyword list.
practice.solution:
def tokenize(src):
    keywords = ['int', 'float', 'if', 'else', 'while', 'return']
    two = ['==', '!=', '<=', '>=']
    one = '+-*/=<>!'
    punct = ';,(){}'
    out = []
    i = 0
    n = len(src)
    while i < n:
        c = src[i]
        if c.isspace():
            i += 1
        elif c.isalpha() or c == '_':
            j = i
            while j < n and (src[j].isalpha() or src[j].isdigit() or src[j] == '_'):
                j += 1
            word = src[i:j]
            out.append(['KEYWORD' if word in keywords else 'ID', word])
            i = j
        elif c.isdigit():
            j = i
            while j < n and src[j].isdigit():
                j += 1
            out.append(['NUM', src[i:j]])
            i = j
        elif src[i:i + 2] in two:
            out.append(['OP', src[i:i + 2]])
            i += 2
        elif c in one:
            out.append(['OP', c])
            i += 1
        elif c in punct:
            out.append(['PUNCT', c])
            i += 1
        else:
            out.append(['ERROR', c])
            i += 1
    return out

summary: The lexical analyzer must recognize a finite set of valid lexemes of the language. Regular expressions define patterns for strings of symbols. The grammar they define is a regular grammar and the language is a regular language.

Operations on languages are union, concatenation and Kleene closure. A regular expression built with them denotes a language. The star has the highest precedence, then concatenation, and union has the lowest. All are left associative.

Shorthands such as plus, question mark and character ranges are common. Tokens like identifiers and decimal numbers are written with them: letter followed by letters or digits, and an optional sign followed by one or more digits.

keyPoints: Operations: union, concatenation, Kleene closure.
Precedence: star, then concatenation, then union.
x* is zero or more; x+ is one or more; x? is zero or one.

Decimal = (sign)? (digit)+.

items: The lexical analyzer needs to scan and identify only a finite set of valid strings, tokens or lexemes that belong to the language in hand. It searches for the pattern defined by the language rules.

Regular expressions can express finite languages by defining a pattern for finite strings of symbols. The grammar defined by regular expressions is known as regular grammar. The language defined by a regular grammar is known as a regular language.

Regular expression is an important notation for specifying patterns. Each pattern matches a set of strings, so regular expressions serve as names for sets of strings. Programming language tokens can be described by regular languages.
Their definition is recursive, they are easy to understand, and they have an efficient implementation.
There are algebraic laws that regular expressions obey, which can be used to turn them into equivalent forms.

The operations on languages are as follows. The union of two languages L and M is the set of strings in L or in M. The concatenation LM is the set of strings st where s is in L and t is in M. The Kleene closure of L is zero or more occurrences of strings from L.

lesson.tex: \begin{gathered} L \cup M = \{\, s \mid s \in L \text{ or } s \in M \,\} \\[0.6em] LM = \{\, st \mid s \in L,\ t \in M \,\} \\[0.6em] L^{*} = \bigcup_{i \ge 0} L^{i} \end{gathered}

items: Notation: if r and s are regular expressions denoting the languages L of r and L of s, then r or s is a regular expression for the union, r followed by s denotes the concatenation, r star denotes the closure, and a parenthesized r denotes the same language as r.

Precedence and associativity. The star, concatenation and the pipe are left associative. The star has the highest precedence, concatenation the second highest, and the pipe the lowest. So ab|c* means a followed by b, or any number of c.

Common shorthands. x star generates epsilon, x, xx, xxx and so on. x plus means one or more, the same as x followed by x star. x question mark means at most one. The range a to z is all lower-case English letters, A to Z the upper-case ones, and 0 to 9 the digits.

Now some tokens. Let letter be a to z or A to Z, digit be 0 to 9, and sign be plus or minus. A decimal integer is an optional sign followed by one or more digits. An identifier is a letter followed by any number of letters or digits.

The one problem left is how to verify the validity of a regular expression used to specify patterns. The well-accepted solution is finite automata, the next chapter. In the practice section you test these two token patterns by hand and list a Kleene closure.

summary: A finite automaton is a state machine that takes a string of symbols and changes state for each symbol. It is a recognizer for regular expressions. If the whole input is processed and the automaton is in a final state, the string is accepted as a valid token.
It consists of a finite set of states, a finite input alphabet, one start state, a set of final states and a transition function that maps a state and a symbol to a state.
A lexer built on automata implements the longest match rule by running as far as it can and remembering the last point at which it was in a final state.

A circle in the diagram; the machine is in exactly one state at a time.
The state where the machine begins, marked with an arrow.
A state where the input is accepted; drawn with a double circle.
A move from one state to another on an input symbol; it may stay in the same state.
The mapping delta from a state and a symbol to the next state.

keyPoints: The model: Q, the alphabet, q0, the final states and delta.
delta maps Q times the alphabet to Q.

Longest match: keep going, remember the last accepting position.

items: A finite automaton is a state machine that takes a string of symbols as input and changes its state accordingly. It is a recognizer for regular expressions. When a string is fed to it, it changes state for each symbol.
If the input is successfully processed and the automaton reaches a final state, the string is accepted, meaning it is a valid token of the language in hand.

The mathematical model has five parts. A finite set of states, Q. A finite set of input symbols, Sigma. One start state, q0. A set of final states. And a transition function, delta, which maps states and symbols to states.

Construction. States are circles with the name inside. The start state has an arrow pointing to it. A final state is drawn as a double circle. A transition is a directed arrow, taken when the desired symbol appears in the input.
The automaton can move to the next state or stay in the same state, drawn as an arrow from a state to itself.

A note about one claim in the tutorial. It says a final state has an odd number of incoming arrows and an even number of outgoing arrows, with odd one greater than even. That is not a rule of automata. A final state can have any number of arrows in and out. Do not rely on it.

Example. Take an automaton that accepts any three-digit binary value ending in the digit 1. It needs a state for each number of digits read. After the third digit it accepts only if that digit was 1, and a fourth digit is not allowed.
A dead state, which can never reach acceptance, is how a complete table rejects.

lesson.code:
state  on 0   on 1
q0     q1     q1
q1     q2     q2
q2     x      q3     # third digit: only a 1 reaches the accepting state
q3     x      x      # accepting, but a fourth digit is not allowed
x      x      x      # dead state: everything is rejected from here

items: States q0, q1 and q2 count the digits read so far, q3 means three digits read ending in 1, and x is a dead state that absorbs everything else. The practice section gives you this machine as data, and you write the runner.
Now the longest match rule again. A lexer built from automata runs the automaton as long as it can make a transition. Each time it is in a final state it remembers the position.
When the machine gets stuck, the lexer returns the lexeme up to the last remembered final position and restarts from there.

Rule priority fits the same picture. If two token automata both accept the same lexeme, the one listed first, for example the keyword, wins. In the practice section you write the runner, then the longest accepted prefix.

summary: Syntax analysis, or parsing, is the second phase. A lexer cannot check balanced parentheses because regular expressions are too weak, so the parser uses a context-free grammar, recognized by push-down automata.

A grammar has non-terminals, terminals, productions and a start symbol. A derivation replaces non-terminals step by step, left-most or right-most; a parse tree depicts it. A grammar with two parse trees for one string is ambiguous, which is fixed with precedence and associativity or a rewrite.

Top-down parsers need grammars without left recursion and with common prefixes factored out. FIRST and FOLLOW sets are the ingredients of parsing tables. Syntax analysis cannot check declarations or types; the semantic analyzer does.

items: Syntax analysis, or parsing, is the second phase of a compiler. We have seen that a lexical analyzer identifies tokens with regular expressions and pattern rules. But it cannot check the syntax of a sentence, because regular expressions cannot check balancing tokens such as parentheses.

So this phase uses a context-free grammar, a CFG, which is recognized by push-down automata. A CFG is a superset of regular grammar: every regular grammar is also context-free, but some problems are beyond regular grammar. A CFG is a helpful tool for describing the syntax of programming languages.

A context-free grammar has four components. A set of non-terminals, syntactic variables that denote sets of strings. A set of terminals, the tokens, from which strings are formed. A set of productions that say how terminals and non-terminals combine; each has a left side, an arrow and a right side.
And a start symbol, one of the non-terminals, where derivation begins.
Strings are derived from the start symbol by repeatedly replacing a non-terminal with the right side of one of its productions.

Example: palindromes. The language of strings equal to their reverse cannot be described by a regular expression, but a grammar can. Let Q be the start symbol with the productions Q to Z, Q to N, Q to epsilon, Z to 0 Q 0 and N to 1 Q 1. It generates strings like 1001, 11100111 and 0110.

A correction to the tutorial. It lists 00100, 1010101 and 11111 as generated by this grammar. They are not: every production adds a symbol on both ends, so this grammar only produces palindromes of even length. To get odd-length ones you add the productions Q to 0 and Q to 1.
The practice section tests exactly this.

A syntax analyzer, or parser, takes the token stream from the lexical analyzer and checks it against the production rules to detect errors. Its output is a parse tree. So the parser has two tasks: parse the code looking for errors, and generate a parse tree.
Parsers are expected to parse the whole code even if there are errors, using error recovery strategies, which a later chapter covers.
A derivation is a sequence of production applications that yields the input string. At each step there are two decisions: which non-terminal to replace, and which production to use.

In a left-most derivation the left-most non-terminal is always replaced; in a right-most derivation, the right-most one. The sentential forms they produce are called left-sentential and right-sentential forms.

Example: productions E to E plus E, E to E times E, and E to id, with the input id plus id times id. One left-most derivation is E, E plus E, id plus E, id plus E times E, id plus id times E, id plus id times id.

A right-most derivation of the same string is E, E plus E, E plus E times E, E plus E times id, E plus id times id, id plus id times id. Both build the tree where times is below plus. The tutorial's first derivation instead starts with E times E, which is the other tree.
That is ambiguity, covered below.

A parse tree is a graphical depiction of a derivation. The start symbol becomes the root. All leaf nodes are terminals, all interior nodes are non-terminals, and reading the leaves left to right gives the input string.
A parse tree shows associativity and precedence: the deepest sub-tree is evaluated first, so its operator binds tighter.

A grammar is ambiguous if it has more than one parse tree for at least one string. Take E to E plus E, E to E minus E and E to id. For id plus id minus id, there are two trees, grouping the plus first or the minus first. An ambiguous grammar is not good for compiler construction.
No method can detect and remove ambiguity automatically. It can be removed by rewriting the grammar, or by setting associativity and precedence constraints.

Associativity decides which operator takes an operand that has operators on both sides. Addition, subtraction, multiplication and division are left associative, so id op id op id is evaluated as (id op id) op id. Exponentiation is right associative, evaluated as id op (id op id).

Precedence decides which operator takes a shared operand. The expression 2+3*4 has two trees, one for (2+3)*4 and one for 2+(3*4). Setting the precedence of times above plus removes the ambiguity: the expression is always read as 2 + (3 * 4).

Left recursion. A grammar is left-recursive if some non-terminal A derives a string whose left-most symbol is A itself. Top-down parsers start from the start symbol, and when they meet the same non-terminal first again, they cannot judge when to stop and loop forever.
A to A alpha or beta is immediate left recursion. S to A alpha or beta together with A to S d is indirect.

To remove immediate left recursion, convert A to A alpha or beta into A to beta A' and A' to alpha A' or epsilon. The language is unchanged. For indirect recursion, order the non-terminals, substitute earlier ones into later productions, then remove immediate recursion.
For S to A alpha or beta and A to S d, substituting gives A to A alpha d or beta d, which becomes A to beta d A' and A' to alpha d A' or epsilon.

Left factoring. If more than one production for a non-terminal shares a prefix, a top-down parser cannot decide which to use. For A to alpha beta or alpha gamma, rewrite as A to alpha A' and A' to beta or gamma. Now there is one production per prefix.

FIRST and FOLLOW. These sets are an important part of building a parsing table. FIRST of a symbol is the set of terminals that can begin a string derived from it, plus epsilon if it can derive the empty string. A terminal's FIRST set is itself.
If a production X to Y1 Y2 and so on exists, FIRST of Y1 is in FIRST of X, and if Y1 can derive epsilon, then FIRST of Y2 as well, and so on.

FOLLOW of a non-terminal is the set of terminals that can immediately follow it in some sentential form. The start symbol has the end marker, written dollar. If A to alpha B beta, then FIRST of beta, except epsilon, is in FOLLOW of B.
If beta can vanish, or is empty, then FOLLOW of A is in FOLLOW of B.

lesson.tex: \begin{gathered} \mathrm{FIRST}(\alpha) = \{\, t \mid \alpha \Rightarrow^{*} t\beta \,\} \cup \{\, \varepsilon \mid \alpha \Rightarrow^{*} \varepsilon \,\} \\[0.6em] \mathrm{FOLLOW}(A) = \{\, t \mid S \Rightarrow^{*} \alpha A t \beta \,\} \end{gathered}

items: Limitations. Syntax analyzers receive tokens from lexical analyzers. They cannot determine whether a token is valid, whether it is declared before use, whether it is initialized, or whether an operation on its type is valid. The semantic analyzer does those tasks.

The practice section tests the palindrome grammar, counts the parse trees of an ambiguous grammar, removes left recursion, factors a common prefix, and computes FIRST and FOLLOW for the standard expression grammar.

summary: Parsers follow the production rules of a context-free grammar. How the rules are applied divides parsing into two kinds: top-down and bottom-up.

Top-down parsing starts from the start symbol and tries to transform it into the input, building the tree from the root. A common form is recursive descent, which can need backtracking: if one production fails, the parser restarts with another production of the same non-terminal.
Bottom-up parsing starts from the input symbols and builds the tree up to the start symbol, by finding right sides in the input and replacing them with left sides.

Builds the parse tree from the input symbols up to the start symbol.
A top-down parser with one recursive procedure per non-terminal.
Trying the next production when one fails, possibly reading input more than once.
Replacing the right side of a production found in the input with its left side.

keyPoints: The two kinds: top-down and bottom-up.

items: Syntax analyzers follow production rules defined by a context-free grammar. The way the production rules are implemented, the derivation, divides parsing into two types: top-down parsing and bottom-up parsing.

When the parser starts constructing the parse tree from the start symbol and then tries to transform the start symbol into the input, it is called top-down parsing. Recursive descent parsing is a common form.
It is called recursive because it uses recursive procedures to process the input, and it suffers from backtracking.

Backtracking means that if one derivation of a production fails, the syntax analyzer restarts the process using different rules of the same production. This may process the input string more than once to determine the right production.
Example. The grammar S to r X d or r Z d, X to o a or e a, Z to a i. The input is read. The parser starts with S and matches the left-most letter r using S to r X d. It advances to e.
It expands X with its first production X to o a, which does not match, so it backtracks to the next production X to e a. Now all letters match in order, and the string is accepted.
Bottom-up parsing, as the name suggests, starts with the input symbols and tries to construct the parse tree up to the start symbol.

Example. Input a plus b times c, with productions S to E, E to E plus T, E to E times T, E to T and T to id. The parser reads the input and checks whether any right side matches. Each id is replaced by T, the first T by E, the pair E plus T by E, and so on, until E and then S remain.
Every step is a reduction, the reverse of a derivation step.

lesson.code:
a + b * c
T + b * c
E + b * c
E + T * c
E * c
E * T
E
S

items: Look closely at this trace. It reduces E plus T to E in the fourth line, which makes the sum the left operand of the times: it groups a plus b first. That is a quirk of the tutorial's ambiguous grammar, where E to E plus T and E to E times T have the same level.
A grammar with separate levels for times and plus, as in later chapters, groups b times c first.
In the practice section you write the backtracking recognizer and count how many productions it tries. Then the next chapters take the top-down and bottom-up families apart.

summary: Top-down parsing builds the tree from the root toward the leaves. A recursive descent parser uses procedures for each terminal and non-terminal, and may need backtracking unless the grammar is left factored.

A predictive parser is a recursive descent parser that predicts which production to use, using a look-ahead pointer, and never backtracks. It accepts only LL(k) grammars. It can be table driven: a stack and a parsing table decide each step.
In LL(k) the first L is for left-to-right input, the second for a left-most derivation, and k is the number of look-ahead symbols. Usually k is 1.

The next input symbol(s) the parser examines before choosing a production.

items: The top-down parsing technique parses the input and starts constructing a parse tree from the root node, gradually moving down to the leaf nodes. The main types are recursive descent parsing and predictive parsing.

Recursive descent is a top-down technique that constructs the parse tree from the top, reading input from left to right. It uses a procedure for every terminal and non-terminal entity. It recursively parses the input, which may or may not require backtracking.
A grammar that is not left factored cannot avoid backtracking. A form of recursive descent that does not require backtracking is known as predictive parsing.

Here is a recursive descent parser in miniature, for arithmetic. The grammar is E to T plus T and so on, T to F times F and so on, F to a number or a parenthesized E. Each rule becomes a function. Because times is handled one level below plus, precedence comes out right.
Loops replace the left-recursive rules, which a recursive descent parser cannot use directly.

lesson.code:
def expr(p):            # E -> T ('+' T)*
    v = term(p)
    while p.peek() == '+':
        p.next(); v = v + term(p)
    return v

items: Back-tracking recap: top-down parsers start from the start symbol and match the input against the production rules. If a rule fails, they back up. The cost is time, and the effect on any side actions.

A predictive parser is a recursive descent parser that can predict which production to use to replace the input string. It does not suffer from backtracking. To do this it uses a look-ahead pointer, which points to the next input symbols, and it puts constraints on the grammar.
It accepts only a class of grammars known as LL(k).

Predictive parsing uses a stack and a parsing table to parse the input and generate a parse tree. Both the stack and the input contain an end symbol, dollar, to denote that the stack is empty and the input is consumed. The parser consults the table for the combination of stack top and input symbol.
In recursive descent, there may be more than one production to choose from; in a predictive parser, each step has at most one. If there is none, parsing fails.

An LL parser accepts LL grammar. LL grammar is a subset of context-free grammar with restrictions that make it easy to implement. It can be implemented by recursive descent or by a table-driven algorithm.
It is written LL(k): the first L means the input is parsed left to right, the second L means a left-most derivation, and k is the number of look-ahead symbols. Generally k is 1.
We stay with deterministic LL(1) for explanation, since the table size grows exponentially with k. And if a grammar is not LL(1), it is usually not LL(k) for any k.

The LL(1) algorithm. Start with dollar and the start symbol on the stack, and the input followed by dollar. Repeat: let X be the top of the stack and a the current input symbol. If X is a terminal or dollar: if X equals a, pop it and advance the input; otherwise it is an error.

If X is a non-terminal: look up M[X, a]. If it holds the production X to Y1 Y2 up to Yk, pop X, push Yk down to Y1 so that Y1 is on top, and output the production. If the entry is empty, it is an error. Stop when X is dollar.

A grammar G is LL(1) if, for any two distinct productions A to alpha and A to beta, three things hold: no terminal a starts a string derived from both alpha and beta; at most one of them can derive the empty string; and if beta can derive empty, alpha derives no string beginning with a terminal in FOLLOW of A.

The standard expression table is built from the FIRST and FOLLOW sets of the earlier chapter: put the production A to alpha in M[A, a] for each a in FIRST of alpha, and if alpha can vanish, for each a in FOLLOW of A.
In the practice section you get that table as data and write the algorithm, plus a recursive descent evaluator.

Shift-reduce parsing | uses | Shift step and reduce step
Reduce step | replaces | Handle with left side
LR parser | is | Non-recursive shift-reduce parser
LR parser | builds | Right-most derivation in reverse
SLR LR(1) and LALR | are | LR parser constructions

summary: Bottom-up parsing starts from the leaves and works upward to the root: it starts with a sentence and applies productions in reverse to reach the start symbol.

Shift-reduce parsing has two steps. A shift moves the next input symbol onto the stack. A reduce, when the top of the stack holds a handle (a complete right side), pops it and pushes the left-side non-terminal.

The LR parser is a non-recursive shift-reduce parser. It reads input left to right and builds a right-most derivation in reverse. Three constructions are common: SLR(1), LR(1) and LALR(1), trading table size against the class of grammars they handle.

glossary.def: Move the next input symbol onto the stack.
Replace a handle on the stack top by the left side of its production.
A right side of a production that sits on top of the stack and can be reduced.
A table-driven shift-reduce parser: Left-to-right scan, Right-most derivation in reverse.
Simple LR: smallest class of grammars, few states, simple and fast to build.
Canonical LR: complete set of LR(1) grammars, large table, slow construction.
Look-ahead LR: intermediate class, the same number of states as SLR(1).

keyPoints: Shift pushes an input symbol; reduce pops a handle and pushes the left side.
Bottom-up parsing runs a right-most derivation backwards.
LR uses action and goto tables.
SLR(1) is simplest; LR(1) most powerful; LALR(1) in between.
LL expands non-terminals and builds top-down; LR reduces and builds bottom-up.
LR can handle a larger class of grammars than LL.

items: Bottom-up parsing starts from the leaf nodes of a tree and works upward until it reaches the root node. We start from a sentence and apply production rules in reverse to reach the start symbol.

Shift-reduce parsing uses two unique steps. The shift step advances the input pointer to the next input symbol, called the shifted symbol, and pushes it onto the stack. The shifted symbol is treated as a single node of the parse tree.
The reduce step happens when the parser finds a complete grammar rule, a handle, on top of the stack: it pops the handle and replaces it with the left-side non-terminal.
The LR parser is a non-recursive, shift-reduce, bottom-up parser. It uses a wide class of context-free grammars, which makes it the most efficient syntax analysis technique of the family.

LR parsers are also known as LR(k) parsers, where L stands for left-to-right scanning of the input, R stands for constructing a right-most derivation in reverse, and k is the number of look-ahead symbols.
Three widely used algorithms construct an LR parser. SLR(1), simple LR: it works on the smallest class of grammars, has few states and so a very small table, and its construction is simple and fast.

LR(1), canonical LR: it works on the complete set of LR(1) grammars, but generates a large table and many states, and construction is slow. LALR(1), look-ahead LR: it works on an intermediate class of grammars and has the same number of states as SLR(1).

The skeleton of the LR algorithm. Read a token. Repeat: look at the state s on top of the stack and the action for s and the token. If the action is shift to state si, push the token and si, and read the next token.

If it is reduce A to beta, pop twice the length of beta symbols, look at the state now on top, push A, and push the goto entry for that state and A. If it is accept, return. Otherwise report an error.
A worked table. Grammar: rule 1 is E to E plus T, rule 2 is E to T, rule 3 is T to id. The tables below are the SLR(1) tables. The practice section runs them.

lesson.code:
state   id    +     $     |  E   T
0       s3                    |  1   2
1             s4    acc       |
2             r2    r2        |
3             r3    r3        |
4       s3                    |      5
5             r1    r1        |

items: Running id plus id: shift id to state 3, reduce T to id, go to state 2, reduce E to T, go to state 1, shift the plus to state 4, shift id to state 3, reduce T to id, go to state 5, reduce E to E plus T, go to state 1, accept on dollar.

LL versus LR. An LL parser does a left-most derivation; an LR parser does a right-most derivation in reverse. LL starts with the root non-terminal on the stack and ends when the stack is empty; LR starts with an empty stack and ends with the root non-terminal on the stack.
LL uses the stack for what is still expected; LR uses it for what has already been seen.
LL builds the tree top-down, continuously popping a non-terminal and pushing its right side; it expands non-terminals and reads terminals when it pops them.

LR builds bottom-up, recognizes a right side on the stack, pops it and pushes the non-terminal; it reduces, and reads terminals while pushing them. The LL parser corresponds to a pre-order traversal of the parse tree, LR to a post-order one.

chapters.title: Error recovery and ASTs

maps.title: Errors and trees
links: Parser | detects | Errors and carries on
Error | can be | Lexical, syntactical, semantical or logical
Panic mode | skips to | Delimiter
Statement mode | inserts or replaces | Tokens
Error productions | add | Known erroneous constructs
Global correction | finds | Closest error-free program
Abstract syntax tree | is | Compact parse tree

summary: A parser should detect and report errors and then carry on parsing. Errors arise at several stages: lexical (a misspelled identifier), syntactic (a missing semicolon or unbalanced parenthesis), semantic (an incompatible assignment) and logical (unreachable code, an infinite loop).

Four recovery strategies: panic mode skips input up to a delimiter such as a semicolon; statement mode makes a local correction; error productions add known mistakes to the grammar; global correction finds the closest correct program but is too expensive in practice.
Parse trees contain more detail than later phases need. An abstract syntax tree hides single-child chains and punctuation, leaving only the operators and operands.

glossary.def: On an error, skip input until a delimiter such as a semicolon, then resume.
Make a local fix, such as inserting a missing semicolon, so the rest of the statement can parse.
A grammar rule added for a common mistake so the parser can recognize and report it.
Find the closest error-free program to the erroneous one; not used in practice.
A tree with the essential structure only: operators as nodes and operands as children.
Such as an identifier typed incorrectly.
Such as unreachable code or an infinite loop.

keyPoints: Errors: lexical, syntactical, semantical, logical.
Panic mode is the simplest and cannot loop forever.
Statement mode can loop if a correction is wrong.
Error productions describe expected mistakes.
Global correction is too costly for practice.
ASTs are smaller than parse trees and easier for later phases.

items: A parser should be able to detect and report any error in the program. When an error is encountered, it should be able to handle it and carry on parsing the rest of the input. Mostly the parser checks for errors, but errors may be encountered at various stages of compilation.

A program may have these kinds of errors. Lexical: the name of an identifier typed incorrectly. Syntactical: a missing semicolon or unbalanced parenthesis. Semantical: an incompatible value assignment. Logical: unreachable code or an infinite loop.

There are four common error recovery strategies. Panic mode: when the parser meets an error anywhere in a statement, it ignores the rest of the statement, not processing input from the erroneous token to a delimiter such as a semicolon.
It is the easiest way of error recovery and it prevents the parser from developing infinite loops.

Statement mode: when the parser encounters an error, it tries to take corrective measures so that the rest of the statement allows the parser to parse ahead. For example, inserting a missing semicolon or replacing a comma by a semicolon.
Parser designers must be careful, because one wrong correction may lead to an infinite loop.

Error productions: some common errors are known to compiler designers. They can create an augmented grammar with productions that generate those erroneous constructs, to be used when the errors are encountered.

Global correction: the parser considers the program as a whole and tries to work out what it is intended to do, finding the closest match that is error-free. For an erroneous input X it creates a parse tree for some closest error-free statement Y, which allows minimal changes to the source.
But because of its time and space complexity, it has not been implemented in practice.

Now abstract syntax trees. A parse tree is not easy for the compiler to work with, because it contains more detail than needed. Most leaf nodes are single children of their parents, such as an identifier below a factor below a term below an expression.

That information can be eliminated before the tree is fed to the next phase. Hiding the extra information gives an abstract syntax tree, in which operators are the nodes and operands are their children.

ASTs are important data structures in a compiler, with the least unnecessary information. They are more compact than parse trees and can be used more easily by the compiler. For a plus b times c, the AST is a plus node with the leaf a on the left and a times node with leaves b and c on the right.

The practice section has three labs: panic mode recovery that reports one error per statement and moves on, the stack-based parenthesis check that regular expressions cannot do, and building an AST with precedence from a token list.

chapters.title: Semantic analysis

maps.title: Semantic analysis
links: Semantic analysis | uses | Syntax directed definitions
Syntax directed definition | is | Grammar plus semantic rules
Semantic analysis | checks | Scope, types and array bounds
Attribute grammar | attaches | Attributes to non-terminals
Synthesized attribute | takes values from | Children
Inherited attribute | takes values from | Parent and siblings
S-attributed SDT | uses only | Synthesized attributes
L-attributed SDT | forbids | Values from right siblings

summary: A parse tree alone does not say how to evaluate or interpret anything. Semantics give meaning to the constructs: grammar plus semantic rules is a syntax directed definition.
Semantic analysis checks scope resolution, type checking and array bounds, and reports semantic errors such as type mismatch and undeclared variables.
An attribute grammar attaches attributes to non-terminals. Synthesized attributes take their values from child nodes; inherited attributes take theirs from the parent or siblings.

An S-attributed definition uses only synthesized attributes and is evaluated bottom-up. An L-attributed definition also allows inherited attributes, but never from right siblings, and is evaluated depth-first and left to right. Every S-attributed definition is L-attributed.

glossary.def: The meaning of the constructs: tokens and syntax structure.
A context-free grammar together with semantic rules.
A named value, with a domain such as integer or string, attached to a grammar symbol.
An attribute whose value comes from the node's children.
An attribute whose value comes from the parent or siblings.
Uses only synthesized attributes; evaluated bottom-up.
Uses synthesized and inherited attributes, with no values from right siblings.
A syntax tree carrying attribute values.

keyPoints: CFG + semantic rules = syntax directed definition.
Tasks: scope resolution, type checking, array-bound checking.
Errors: type mismatch, undeclared variable, redeclaration, out-of-scope access, parameter mismatch.
Synthesized: from children. Inherited: from parent and siblings.
S-attributed: bottom-up. L-attributed: depth-first, left to right.
S-attributed implies L-attributed.

items: We have learnt how a parser builds parse trees in syntax analysis. The plain parse tree is of no use to a compiler alone, because it carries no information on how to evaluate it. The productions of a context-free grammar make the rules of the language, but they do not say how to interpret them.
For example, the production E to E plus T has no semantic rule attached, so it cannot help make any sense of the production.

Semantics of a language provide meaning to its constructs, like tokens and syntax structure. They help interpret symbols, their types and their relations. Semantic analysis judges whether the syntax structure built in the source program derives any meaning.
A grammar plus semantic rules is called a syntax directed definition.

Take the declaration int a = followed by a string literal. It passes lexical analysis and syntax analysis, because it is lexically and structurally correct. But it should give a semantic error, because the type of the assignment differs.
These rules are set by the grammar of the language and evaluated in semantic analysis.
The semantic analyzer performs scope resolution, type checking and array-bound checking.

The semantic errors it should recognize are: type mismatch, an undeclared variable, misuse of a reserved identifier, multiple declaration of a variable in a scope, access to an out-of-scope variable, and a mismatch between actual and formal parameters.

An attribute grammar is a special form of context-free grammar where additional information, attributes, is appended to some non-terminals to provide context-sensitive information. Each attribute has a well-defined domain of values, such as integer, float, character, string or expression.
It is a medium to give semantics to the CFG, and viewed as a parse tree, it can pass values or information among the nodes.

lesson.tex: \begin{gathered} E \rightarrow E + T \\[0.6em] \{\; E.value = E.value + T.value \;\} \end{gathered}

items: In this rule, the values of E and T are added, and the result is copied to the left non-terminal E. Attributes are assigned values from their domain at parse time and evaluated at the time of assignment or conditions. By how they get values, attributes fall into two kinds.

Synthesized attributes get values from the attribute values of their child nodes. For the production S to A B C, if S takes its value from A, B and C, then it is a synthesized attribute. They never take values from parent or sibling nodes.
In E to E plus T the parent E gets its value from its children.

Inherited attributes, in contrast, can take values from the parent or siblings. In S to A B C, A can get values from S, B and C; B from S, A and C; and C from S, A and B. A typical example is the type in a declaration: in int a, b, c, the type is carried down to each name in the list.

Terms used when parsing with actions. Expansion is when a non-terminal is expanded to terminals by a grammar rule. Reduction is when terminals are reduced to their non-terminal. Whenever a reduction occurs, its semantic rules, the actions, are applied.

The semantic analyzer receives the AST from syntax analysis and attaches attribute information to it, giving the attributed AST. An attribute is a pair of name and value, such as type integer or present value 5.

An S-attributed SDT uses only synthesized attributes. These are evaluated with semantic actions written after the right side of the production. Attributes in S-attributed SDTs are evaluated during bottom-up parsing, since parent values depend on child values.

An L-attributed SDT uses both synthesized and inherited attributes, with the restriction of not taking values from right siblings. For S to A B C: S can take values from A, B and C. A can take values from S only. B can take values from S and A. C can take values from S, A and B.
No non-terminal takes a value from a sibling to its right. They are evaluated depth-first and left to right. Every S-attributed definition is also L-attributed.
In the practice section you write a small type checker with a symbol table, evaluate synthesized attributes on an expression tree, and pass an inherited type down a declaration list.

quiz.explain: Evaluation is depth-first, left to right.

quiz.explain: The syntax is fine; the meaning is not.

practice.solution:
def inherit_types(decl):
    parts = decl.strip().split(None, 1)
    t = parts[0]
    names = parts[1].split(',') if len(parts) > 1 else []
    return [[n.strip(), t] for n in names if n.strip()]

chapters.title: Runtime environment

maps.title: Runtime environment
links: Procedure activation | has | Activation record
Activation record | lives on | Control stack
Activations | form | Activation tree
Code | uses | Static allocation
Procedure calls | use | Stack allocation
Dynamic variables | use | Heap allocation
Parameter passing | has modes | Value, reference, copy-restore, name

summary: A program needs memory and a mapping from names to locations at run time. The runtime environment is the state of the target machine, and the runtime support system handles memory allocation and de-allocation while the program runs.

Each procedure execution is an activation with an activation record on the control stack, holding temporaries, local data, machine status, links, parameters and the return value. The sequence of activations forms an activation tree.
Code is allocated statically, procedure activations on a stack and dynamic data on a heap.
Parameters are passed by value, by reference, by copy-restore or by name. They differ in whether the callee can change the caller's variable and when.

glossary.def: The state of the target machine while the program runs: libraries, variables and memory.
One execution of a procedure.
The data needed for one call: temporaries, locals, machine status, links, parameters, return value.
The stack on which activation records are kept.
A tree showing how procedure calls nest.
The value of an expression.
The memory location where an expression's value is stored.
A variable in the definition of the called procedure.
A value or address passed in the call.
The r-value is copied; changes inside do not affect the caller.
The l-value is passed; the callee works on the caller's variable.
Values are copied in, and copied back to the caller's variables when the procedure ends.
The argument expression is substituted textually into the body.

keyPoints: Activation records live on the control stack.
The call order gives a depth-first activation tree.
Static: code, global data. Stack: procedure calls. Heap: dynamic data.
Stack and heap sit at opposite ends of memory and grow toward each other.
r-value is a value; l-value is a location. 7 = x + y is an l-value error.
Value does not change the caller; reference does; copy-restore does at the end; name substitutes text.

items: A program as source code is merely a collection of text. To make it alive, it requires actions performed on the target machine, and it needs memory resources to execute instructions. Names of procedures and identifiers must be mapped to actual memory locations at run time.

By runtime we mean a program in execution. The runtime environment is a state of the target machine, which may include software libraries, environment variables and so on, to provide services to the processes running in the system.

The runtime support system is a package, mostly generated with the executable itself, that handles communication between the process and the runtime environment. It takes care of memory allocation and de-allocation while the program is executing.

A program is a sequence of instructions combined into procedures. Instructions in a procedure execute sequentially. The execution of a procedure is called its activation. An activation record contains all the information needed to call a procedure.
Depending on the language it may contain these units.

lesson.code:
Temporaries         intermediate values of expressions
Local data          locals of the called procedure
Machine status      registers, program counter before the call
Control link        address of the caller's activation record
Access link         data outside the local scope
Actual parameters   inputs sent to the called procedure
Return value        value returned to the caller

items: Whenever a procedure is executed, its activation record is stored on the stack, also known as the control stack. When a procedure calls another, the caller's execution is suspended until the called procedure finishes, and the called procedure's record is pushed on the stack.
When control flows sequentially, with a call transferring control to the callee and the return giving it back, the series of activations can be drawn as a tree, the activation tree.

In the tutorial's example, the main program prints a prompt, reads a name, calls show_data and prints a last message; show_data is a child of main in the tree. The tutorial's code uses two different names for the same parameter, user and username; take it as one variable.
Procedures are executed depth first, so stack allocation is the best suited storage for procedure activations.
The runtime environment manages memory for these entities. Code is the text part of the program, which does not change at run time, and its memory requirement is known at compile time.

Procedures have static text but are called in a random manner, so stack storage is used to manage their calls and activations. Variables are known only at run time unless they are global or constant, and a heap scheme manages their allocation and de-allocation.

In static allocation, compilation data is bound to a fixed location in memory and does not change while the program runs. As the memory requirement and locations are known in advance, no runtime support for allocation and de-allocation is needed.
Stack allocation manages procedure calls and activations. It works last in, first out, and it is very useful for recursive calls.
Heap allocation is used to dynamically allocate memory to variables whose lifetime is not tied to a call, and claim it back when they are no longer required.

Except for statically allocated memory, both stack and heap can grow and shrink dynamically and unexpectedly, so they cannot be given a fixed amount of memory. The text part has a fixed area. Stack and heap are placed at the two extremes of the program's memory and grow toward each other.
Now parameter passing: the communication medium among procedures. First some terms. The value of an expression is its r-value. A single variable on the right of an assignment also gives an r-value.

The location where an expression is stored is its l-value, which always appears on the left of an assignment. In day = 1 and week = day * 7, the constants and the variables have r-values; only variables have l-values.
The statement 7 = x + y is an l-value error, because the constant 7 has no memory location.

Formal parameters are the variables in the definition of the called function that take the information passed by the caller. Actual parameters are the values or addresses given in the call. What the formal parameter holds depends on the technique, a value or an address.

Pass by value: the caller passes the r-value of the actual parameters and the compiler places it in the callee's activation record. If the formal parameter is changed, the actual parameter is not affected.

Pass by reference: the l-value of the actual parameter is copied into the callee's activation record. The callee has the address of the actual parameter, so a change to the formal parameter is seen on the actual parameter.
Pass by copy-restore works like reference, except that the changes to the actual parameters are made only when the called procedure ends. On entry the values are copied in.
Changes to the formal parameter have no immediate effect on the actual parameter, but when the procedure ends the formal's value is copied to the actual's location.

The tutorial's example: y is a global set to 10, and the procedure takes x, sets x to 99 and then sets y to 0. Under copy-restore, at the end x is copied back into y, so the caller prints 99. The practice section runs this example under each mode.

Pass by name, from languages like Algol, works like the C preprocessor. The argument expression is substituted textually for the formal parameter in the body of the procedure, so it works on the actual parameters much like pass by reference.
The practice section builds an activation tree from call and return events and runs the parameter modes.

quiz.q: Where are activation records stored?
quiz.explain: Calls are last in, first out.

quiz.q: Which part of a program uses static allocation?
quiz.explain: Its size is known at compile time.

quiz.q: In pass by value, a change to the formal parameter...
quiz.explain: Only the r-value was copied.

quiz.q: Why is 7 = x + y an error?
quiz.explain: A constant is not a memory location.

cards.a: Calls nest depth first, so last in first out.
Values are copied back when the procedure ends.

cards.q: Which end do stack and heap start at?
cards.a: Opposite ends of the program's memory.

practice.intro: Events are strings "call NAME" and "return". The first event is the call of the root. Write activation_tree(events): return the tree as [name, [children]] with the children in call order.
practice.hint: Keep a stack of open nodes. A call creates a node under the top of the stack; a return pops.

practice.intro: Same events. Write max_depth(events): the largest number of activation records on the stack at one time.
practice.hint: Count calls up and returns down; remember the peak.

practice.title: Same call, four modes
practice.intro: A global y starts at 10. The procedure p(x) does: x = 99, then y = 0. The call is p(y). Write final_y(mode) for mode "value", "reference", "copy-restore" or "name": return the value of y after the call. By value, x is a separate copy. By reference and by name, x is the same variable as y. By copy-restore, x is a copy that is stored into y when p ends.
practice.hint: Decide which assignments touch the same variable in each mode. Copy-restore writes x into y at the very end.
practice.solution:
def final_y(mode):
    y = 10
    if mode == 'value':
        x = y
        x = 99
        y = 0
        return y
    if mode == 'reference' or mode == 'name':
        y = 99
        y = 0
        return y
    x = y
    x = 99
    y = 0
    y = x

summary: The symbol table stores information about names: variables, functions, objects, classes and interfaces. It is used by both the analysis and the synthesis parts of the compiler.

It serves to store names in one place, to check that a variable is declared, to type check, and to resolve scope. It is a linear table or, most often, a hash table. Each entry holds the symbol name, type and attributes.

The two operations are insert, used mostly by the analysis phase, and lookup, which returns 0 when the symbol is absent. For scope, tables are arranged in a hierarchy, and lookup searches the current scope first and then the parent scopes.

Adds a new name with its attributes to the table.

The region of a program in which a name is visible.

static int interest is stored as interest, int, static.

lookup checks existence, prior declaration, scope, initialization and duplicates.
Scope lookup: current table first, then parents, up to the global table.

items: The symbol table is an important data structure created and maintained by compilers to store information about the occurrence of various entities such as variable names, function names, objects, classes and interfaces. It is used by both the analysis and synthesis parts of the compiler.

Depending on the language, a symbol table may serve these purposes: to store the names of all entities in a structured form in one place; to verify that a variable has been declared; to implement type checking by verifying that assignments and expressions are semantically correct; and to determine the scope of a name, which is scope resolution.

A symbol table is simply a table, either linear or a hash table. It keeps an entry for each name in the format symbol name, type, attribute. For example the declaration static int interest should be stored as the entry interest, int, static. The attribute field holds the other facts about the name.

Implementation. If a compiler handles only a small amount of data, the table can be an unordered list, which is easy to code but suitable only for small tables. The alternatives are a sorted or unsorted linear list, a binary search tree, and a hash table.
Most symbol tables are hash tables, where the symbol itself is the key of the hash function and the return value is the information about the symbol.

The insert operation is more frequently used by the analysis phase, the first half of the compiler, where tokens are identified and names are stored. It adds information about unique names occurring in the source code.
The attributes of a symbol are the information associated with it, such as its value, state, scope and type. For int a, the compiler calls insert with a and int.

The lookup operation searches for a name to determine whether the symbol exists in the table, whether it is declared before it is used, whether the name is used in the scope, whether the symbol is initialized, and whether it is declared multiple times. The basic form is lookup of a symbol.
It returns 0 if the symbol does not exist, and otherwise the attributes stored in the table.

Scope management. A compiler maintains two kinds of symbol tables: a global symbol table accessible by all procedures, and scope symbol tables created for each scope in the program. To determine the scope of a name, the tables are arranged in a hierarchy.

In the tutorial's example, a global variable value and two procedures pro_one and pro_two sit in the global table. Each procedure has its own table with its locals, and each inner block has a child table. Names in pro_one's table and its children are not available to pro_two.

The hierarchy is kept by the semantic analyzer. To find a name it searches in this order. First the current scope, the current symbol table. If the name is found, the search is finished; otherwise it goes to the parent table, until the name is found or the global table has been searched.

This is what the practice section builds: a scoped table driven by a list of operations. You will see shadowing, where an inner declaration hides an outer one, and the hash function that a real implementation uses.

Intermediate code | can be | High level or low level

summary: Intermediate code lets one analysis front end serve many machines: only the synthesis part changes with the target. It also makes it easier to apply optimizations that are independent of the machine.

It can be high level, close to the source, or low level, close to the machine, and language specific (Java byte code) or language independent (three-address code). Three-address code has at most three addresses per instruction and is stored as quadruples, triples or indirect triples.
Declarations allocate memory to names consecutively, using an offset that starts at zero and grows by each name's width, and enter the name, type and offset into the symbol table.

glossary.def: A program for an abstract machine, between the source and the target.
Close to the source language; easy to generate and to modify.
Close to the target machine; good for register and instruction selection.
Instructions with at most three addresses, such as x = y op z.
An instruction with four fields: operator, arg1, arg2 and result.
An instruction with three fields; the result is referred to by its position.
A list of pointers to triples, so the optimizer can reorder them freely.
The relative address of a name within its data area.

keyPoints: IR saves writing a full compiler for each machine.
Analysis stays the same; only synthesis changes per target.
Three-address code assumes unlimited registers.
Quadruples have a result field; triples use positions; indirect triples use pointers.
Triples are hard to reorder; indirect triples fix that.
Declarations: offset = offset + width.

items: Source code can be translated directly into target machine code. So why have an intermediate code at all? There are reasons. Without it, each new machine would need a full native compiler.
Intermediate code eliminates that, by keeping the analysis portion the same for all the compilers, so only the second part, synthesis, changes with the target machine.
It also becomes easier to apply code optimization techniques to the intermediate code, since the changes to improve performance do not depend on the machine.

Intermediate codes can be represented in a variety of ways. A high-level IR is very close to the source language itself. It can be generated easily from the source code and modified for performance, but it is less preferred for target machine optimization.
A low-level IR is close to the target machine, which makes it suitable for register and memory allocation and instruction set selection. It is good for machine-dependent optimizations.
Intermediate code can be language specific, such as byte code for Java, or language independent, such as three-address code.
The intermediate code generator receives the annotated syntax tree from the semantic analyzer. The tree is converted to a linear representation, such as postfix notation.
Intermediate code tends to be machine independent, so the generator assumes an unlimited number of memory storage units, called registers.

For a = b + c * d, the generator divides the expression into sub-expressions. First c times d goes into a temporary, then b plus that temporary goes into a second, then the result is copied to a. In code, r1 = c * d, then r2 = b + r1, then a = r2.

A correction to the tutorial. Its listing has a third temporary, r3 = r2 + r1, then a = r3. That extra addition does not belong to a = b + c * d. It would compute b + 2 * c * d. The correct code has just the three instructions above, and the practice section generates exactly these.

A three-address code has at most three address locations to calculate the expression. It can be represented in two main forms, quadruples and triples. Each instruction in the quadruple form has four fields: the operator, arg1, arg2 and the result.
For the example: times with c and d giving r1; plus with b and r1 giving r2; and an assignment of r2 to a.

lesson.code:
op   arg1  arg2  result
*    c     d     r1
+    b     r1    r2
=    r2          a

items: Triples have three fields: op, arg1 and arg2. The result of each sub-expression is denoted by the position of the instruction. They are equivalent to a DAG while representing expressions.
Triples face the problem of code immovability during optimization: results are positional, so moving an instruction changes the meaning of every reference to it.

Indirect triples are an enhancement over triples. They use pointers instead of positions to store results. This lets the optimizer reposition sub-expressions freely: it reorders the list of pointers, not the triples.

Declarations. A variable or procedure has to be declared before it can be used. A declaration allocates space in memory and enters the type and name in the symbol table. Taking the program as a collection of procedures, all names can be local to a procedure.

Memory is allocated consecutively, in the order the names are declared, and a variable offset starts at zero as the base address. Because the source language and the target machine may store names differently, relative addressing is used.

The tutorial's example uses C with a 2-byte integer and a 4-byte float, which was true of some old machines; modern compilers use 4 bytes for int. The widths are a parameter, so the rule is the same. Declare int a: the offset is 0, then add the width, so the offset is 2.
Then float b: it is placed at offset 2, and the offset becomes 6.

To enter a name in the symbol table, a procedure called enter is used, with the name, its type and its offset, which is the relative address in the data area. The practice section writes the three-address code generator, the triples generator and the offset allocator.

practice.intro: An expression tree is an atom (a string) or [op, left, right]. Write gen_tac(target, tree). Walk the tree in post-order (left, then right). For each operation emit the quadruple [op, arg1, arg2, temp] where temp is the next of "t1", "t2", ... and an argument is the atom or the temp that holds the sub-result. Finish with ["=", result, "", target]. Return the list of quadruples.
practice.hint: A recursive helper returns the name that holds a sub-tree's value: the atom itself or a new temporary.
practice.solution:
def gen_tac(target, tree):
    code = []
    count = [0]
    def walk(t):
        if isinstance(t, str):
            return t
        a = walk(t[1])
        b = walk(t[2])
        count[0] += 1
        tmp = 't' + str(count[0])
        code.append([t[0], a, b, tmp])
        return tmp
    res = walk(tree)
    code.append(['=', res, '', target])
    return code

practice.intro: Same expression trees. Write gen_triples(target, tree) returning triples [op, arg1, arg2] where a reference to an earlier triple is the string "(i)" with i its 0-based position. Finish with ["=", target, ref] for the final value (use the atom itself if the tree is a single atom).

def gen_triples(target, tree):
    code = []
    def walk(t):
        if isinstance(t, str):
            return t
        a = walk(t[1])
        b = walk(t[2])
        code.append([t[0], a, b])
        return '(' + str(len(code) - 1) + ')'
    res = walk(tree)
    code.append(['=', target, res])
    return code

practice.solution:

    offset = 0
    entries = []
    for name, t in decls:
        entries.append([name, t, offset])
        offset += widths[t]
    return [entries, offset]

summary: Code generation is the final phase. It produces object code in a lower-level language such as assembly, which must carry the exact meaning of the source and be efficient in CPU and memory.

A directed acyclic graph shows how values flow among the statements of a basic block and exposes shared sub-expressions. Peephole optimization improves a small window of code: redundant instructions, unreachable code, jumps to jumps, algebraic simplifications and strength reduction.

A code generator has to select instructions, allocate registers and order instructions. It uses a register descriptor and an address descriptor, and a function getReg picks the register for each result.

glossary.def: A directed acyclic graph of a basic block: leaves are names or constants, interior nodes are operators.
A local optimization over a small portion of code.
An instruction whose effect is already achieved by others.
Code that can never be executed because of the control structure.
Replacing an expensive operation by a cheaper one with the same result.
Records what value each register holds.
Records where the value of each name is currently found.
