keyPoints: The object code must keep the meaning and be efficient.
A DAG shows shared sub-expressions in a basic block.
Peephole: redundant loads, unreachable code, jumps to jumps, algebraic simplification, strength reduction.
x * 2 can become x << 1.
The code generator selects instructions, allocates registers and orders instructions.
Descriptors are updated as code is generated.

items: Code generation can be considered the final phase of compilation. Optimization can still be applied after it, but that can be seen as a part of code generation itself. The code generated by the compiler is object code of some lower-level language, for example assembly language.

A source program in a higher-level language is transformed into lower-level object code, which should have two minimum properties: it should carry the exact meaning of the source code, and it should be efficient in terms of CPU usage and memory management.

A directed acyclic graph, DAG, depicts the structure of a basic block, helps to see the flow of values among the statements, and offers optimization too. It makes transformations on basic blocks easy. Leaf nodes represent identifiers, names or constants. Interior nodes represent operators.
Interior nodes also represent the results of expressions or the names where the values are stored.

Example: t0 = a + b, t1 = t0 + c and d = t0 + t1. The plus node of a and b is reused by both later statements. If the same expression appeared twice with unchanged operands, the DAG would hold one node, which is how common sub-expressions are found.

Peephole optimization works locally on the code to transform it into optimized code. By local we mean a small portion of the code block. It can be applied to intermediate code and to target code. A group of statements is analyzed for these optimizations.

Redundant instruction elimination. At source level the user can simplify code such as y = 10, z = x + y, return z to return x plus 10. At the compiler level, the compiler looks for redundant instructions, such as multiple loading and storing that mean the same even if some are removed.
Move x to R0 followed by move R0 to R1 can be rewritten as move x to R1. That is safe only when R0 is not used afterwards.
Unreachable code is part of the program that is never accessed because of the programming constructs, such as a statement after a return. It can be removed.

Flow of control optimization. The program control may jump back and forth without performing any significant task. A label that only passes control to another label can be bypassed. Given a goto L1 where L1 contains only a goto L2, the first jump can go to L2 directly.

Algebraic expression simplification: a = a + 0 can be replaced by a, and a = a + 1 can be replaced by an increment. Strength reduction replaces operations that consume more time and space with cheaper ones that give the same result. For example, x * 2 can be replaced by x << 1, a single left shift.
And a * a is cheaper than a squared, using a power routine. The tutorial writes a2, meaning the square.
Accessing machine instructions: if the target machine has sophisticated instructions that do specific operations efficiently, using them directly improves the quality of the code.

A code generator needs to understand the target machine's runtime environment and instruction set. It must take these into account. The target language, which may be CISC or RISC. The IR type: an AST, reverse Polish notation or three-address code.

Instruction selection: one IR form can be translated in many ways, and the generator must choose wisely. Register allocation: which values to keep in registers and which registers to use. And ordering of instructions: the order in which instructions execute, a schedule.

The generator tracks registers and addresses with two descriptors. The register descriptor says which registers are available and what each holds. The address descriptor says where the value of each name is: in a register, on the stack, in memory or several of these. They are updated in real time.
For a load LD R1, x, the register descriptor of R1 records that it holds x, and the address descriptor of x records that one copy is in R1.
Where a value is found in several places, the register is preferred over the cache, which is preferred over main memory.

The function getReg decides the location L for the result of x = y op z. If y is already in a register, use that register. Otherwise if a register is available, use it. Otherwise choose a register that requires the fewest loads and stores.

Then the actions for x = y op z. Call getReg to choose L. Find where y is from its address descriptor, and if it is not in L, emit a move of y to L. Find z the same way and emit the operation on z and L.
Now L holds y op z, so update the register descriptor of L to say it holds x, and the address descriptor of x to say it is in L. If y and z have no further use, their registers can be given back.
The practice section writes four peephole passes, a DAG counter that finds common sub-expressions, and a small code generator with descriptors.

summary: Optimization transforms a program so that it uses fewer resources and runs faster, while keeping the meaning, and without slowing the compiler too much. It can be done by the user, on the intermediate code, and on the target code.

Machine-independent optimization works on intermediate code, with no registers or absolute addresses. Machine-dependent optimization uses registers and the memory hierarchy. Basic blocks and the control flow graph structure the program for analysis.

Loops get special attention: moving invariant code out, working with induction variables, and strength reduction. Dead code, partially dead code and partially redundant expressions are removed or moved.

glossary.def: Transforms intermediate code without using CPU registers or absolute memory locations.
Done after target code is generated; uses registers and the memory hierarchy.
A sequence of instructions always executed in order, with no jumps in or out except at its ends.
A graph of basic blocks showing how control passes between them.
Code in a loop that computes the same value on every iteration.
A variable altered in a loop by a loop-invariant amount.
Code that is never executed or whose output is never used.
Code whose result is used only on some paths.
An expression computed more than once on some path without a change in operands.
Moving code to a place where it is computed less often.

keyPoints: Rules: keep the meaning; speed up; be fast itself.
Levels: user code, intermediate code, target code.
Leaders start basic blocks: the first statement, branch targets and statements after a branch.
Loop optimizations: invariant code, induction analysis, strength reduction.
Dead code: unreachable or unused result.
Code motion removes partial redundancy.

items: Optimization is a program transformation technique that tries to improve the code by making it consume fewer resources, such as CPU and memory, and deliver higher speed. High-level general constructs are replaced by very efficient low-level code. A code-optimizing process must follow three rules.

The output code must not in any way change the meaning of the program. Optimization should increase the speed of the program and, if possible, require fewer resources. And optimization should itself be fast, and not delay the overall compiling process.

Efforts can be made at various levels of the compiling process. At the beginning, users can change or rearrange the code or use better algorithms. After generating intermediate code, the compiler can modify it by address calculations and improving loops.
While producing target machine code, the compiler can make use of the memory hierarchy and CPU registers. Optimization is broadly of two types, machine independent and machine dependent.
In machine-independent optimization, the compiler takes the intermediate code and transforms a part that does not involve CPU registers or absolute memory locations.

For example a do-while loop that assigns item = 10 on every iteration before adding it to value can be rewritten with the assignment moved in front of the loop. The repeated assignment of the same value is removed.

Machine-dependent optimization is done after the target code has been generated, when the code is transformed according to the target architecture. It involves CPU registers and may have absolute memory references rather than relative ones.
The optimizers try to take maximum advantage of the memory hierarchy.
Basic blocks. Source code has a number of instructions that are always executed in sequence, and these are considered the basic blocks.

A basic block has no jump statements within it: when the first instruction executes, all the instructions in the block execute in order, with no loss of flow control. Constructs such as if-then-else, switch-case, do-while, for and repeat-until produce basic blocks.

To find the basic blocks, first find the header statements, the leaders. The first statement of the program is a leader. Statements that are the target of any branch, conditional or unconditional, are leaders. Statements that follow a branch statement are leaders.
Each leader and the statements after it, up to the next leader, form a basic block, so a block never contains the header of another block.

Basic blocks play an important role in identifying variables that are used more than once in a single block. If a variable is used more than once, the register allocated to it need not be emptied until the block finishes.
A control flow graph represents the basic blocks of a program, and shows how control is passed among them. It helps optimization by locating unwanted loops in the program.

Loop optimization. Most programs run as a loop in the system, so loops need to be optimized to save CPU cycles and memory. Techniques: invariant code, a fragment inside the loop computing the same value every iteration, can be moved out and computed once.

Induction analysis: a variable is an induction variable if its value is altered within the loop by a loop-invariant value. Strength reduction: an expression such as x * 2 is more expensive than x << 1 and gives the same result, so it is replaced.

Dead-code elimination. Dead code is one or more statements that are either never executed or unreachable, or whose output is never used. Dead code plays no role in any program operation, so it can simply be eliminated.

Partially dead code: some statements compute values that are used only under some circumstances. In the tutorial's flow graph, a variable a is assigned the value of x * y but not used inside the loop, and right after the loop it is reassigned the value of z.
The first assignment is never used, so it can be eliminated. Likewise a conditional statement that is always false means the true branch is never executed and can be removed.

Partial redundancy. A redundant expression is computed more than once on the same path, without a change in operands. A partially redundant expression is computed more than once on some paths, and only once on others.
The tutorial words the two definitions confusingly, but the example makes it clear. Loop-invariant code is partially redundant and can be eliminated by code motion.

If y and z do not change between a and c, then when the condition is true, y OP z is computed twice, otherwise once. Code motion fixes this: compute tmp = y OP z in both branches, assign a = tmp in the true branch, and c = tmp afterwards.
Whichever way the condition goes, y OP z is computed exactly once.
The practice section finds basic blocks, removes dead assignments with a backward pass, and detects loop-invariant statements for code motion.

practice.title: Basic blocks
practice.intro: Code is a list of lines. A label is a line ending in a colon, a jump is "goto L" or "if COND goto L" (the label is the last word). Write basic_blocks(lines): split the code into basic blocks. Leaders: the first line, every label line that some jump targets, and every line after a jump. Return a list of blocks, each a list of lines.
practice.hint: Compute the set of leader indices first. Start a new block at each leader.

practice.title: Dead-code elimination
practice.intro: Statements are [target, uses] where uses is the list of variables the statement reads. Write eliminate_dead(stmts, live_out), where live_out is the list of variables needed after the code. Work backwards: a statement is dead if its target is not live at that point; remove dead statements. Otherwise the target stops being live before it and its uses become live. Return the remaining statements in order.
practice.hint: Loop over the statements backwards, keeping a set of live variables.

practice.title: Loop-invariant statements
practice.intro: A loop body is a list of [target, uses]. A statement is loop-invariant if its target is assigned only once in the loop and every variable it uses is either not assigned in the loop, or assigned by an earlier statement that is itself loop-invariant. Write loop_invariants(body): the 0-based indices of the invariant statements, in order.
practice.hint: A used variable that is assigned in the loop must come from an invariant statement above. Remember that a statement that uses its own target is not invariant.

practice.title: Optimization
practice.text: A basic {{block}} has no jumps inside it. Code that computes the same value every iteration is loop-{{invariant}}. Moving shared computation so it runs once is code {{motion}}.
